html:
The mujahideen were the Islamic guerrilla fighters of Afghanistan who fought the communist government and its Soviet backers from 1979, and then each other after 1992. They were not one army. They were dozens of local bands tied to a handful of parties.

Seven main parties were based in Pakistan, around Peshawar, and only those got foreign weapons. They included Jamiat-e-Islami, whose best field commander was Ahmad Shah Massoud in the Panjshir, and Hizb-i-Islami under Gulbuddin Hekmatyar. Shia groups in the centre and west looked to Iran.

Fighters held the mountains and villages, ambushed convoys and mined roads, while the Soviet army held the cities. Money and arms came through Operation Cyclone and the Pakistani ISI, with Saudi funds. US Stinger missiles, from 1986, made it harder for Soviet helicopters to fly low.

Millions of Afghans fled to camps such as the refugee camps in Pakistan. After the Geneva Accords and the Soviet withdrawal in 1989, the parties took Kabul in 1992 and fell into the civil war that opened the way for the Taliban.
